Catalog Description
Foundations of Money Education. (3-0). Credit 3. Preparation for a financially
challenging world and introduction to concepts and methods of personal financial
planning; financial planning process, time value of money, taxation, credit, housing,
insurance, employee benefits, family economics and building a personal financial plan.
Course Prerequisites
Prerequisite/Corequisite(s): None.
No prior understanding of finance or financial planning is required. This course is
designed to start from the ground up.
Restrictions: Section None
Course Learning Outcomes
Core Objectives:
Critical Thinking Skills: To include creative thinking, innovation, inquiry, and
analysis, evaluation and synthesis of information. 
Critical thinking is essential in the Foundations of Money Education course. Students
learn about a wide array of financial concepts, challenges, decisions, and opportunities
which impact many Americans’ lives (ex. the financial planning process, budgeting,
compound interest, etc.). They then synthesize their knowledge in understanding how
the interaction of each of these will have an aggregate effect on their own wealth and
financial wellness, as well as that of their family and society at large. Students examine
the impact of various financial changes in the economy (ex. inflation, labor markets,
government fiscal policies, etc.) on their lives as individuals and consider actions to
secure and maximize their personal financial wellbeing both now and in the future.
Introduction of real-world applications, data, and news on each subject increase
students’ analytical skills, creative thinking, and appreciation for course concepts.

Communication Skills: To include effective development, interpretation and
expression of ideas through written, oral and visual communication. 
FINP 235 students’ initial financial knowledge is typically limited due to a lack of financial
education in pre-college schooling. Students are forced to recognize this fact during the
first week of class, and so are encouraged to communicate openly and frequently with
their fellow students and instructor(s) in order to most significantly improve their
financial knowledge during the course of the semester. Students communicate with the
instructor through weekly Assignments (some of which include written interpretations
and reflections), during office hour conversations, and via email, and are expected to
ask questions and engage openly during lectures. Through group discussions, think-
pair-share exam reviews, weekly assignments (including financial worksheets, reflection
questions, etc.), and a Reflection Video, students will learn to effectively express their
opinions, concerns, and mastery of critical financial concepts both visually and orally to
the instructor and to their peers.
Empirical and Quantitative Skills: To include the manipulation and analysis of
numerical data or observable facts resulting in informed conclusions. 
A critical component of financial education involves understanding and analyzing data.
Students interpret tables and graphs (ex. historical mortgage rates, inflation rates, etc.),
and use various tools and methods to better understand how financial behavior
impacts individuals, their families, and society at large (ex. retirement planning).
Students learn to understand and use formulas (ex. time value of money, cash
management, etc.), and use computer (ex. Microsoft Excel functions) and web-based
tools (online loan amortization calculators, net pay calculators, etc.) to manipulate and
analyze a variety of scenarios related to debt, investments, inflation, and more. 
Social Responsibility: To include inter-cultural competence, knowledge of civic
responsibility, and the (ability to engage effectively in regional, national, and
global communities. 
Students learn how individuals behave and interact financially with other individuals,
governments, institutions, and society (ex. consumers’ relationship with the economy
and government taxes). Students also learn how the actions of individuals,
corporations, and governments financially impact America and its citizens (ex. bank
failures). While the course is focused on financial concepts, behaviors, challenges, and
opportunities in America, much of what is covered in the course impacts cultures and
nations across the world, and understanding these critical financial concepts can assist
students in engaging effectively with regional, national, and global communities.

Course Learning Outcomes:
Upon completion of this course, students should be able to do the following:
1.  Describe holistic financial planning and the concept of financial literacy
2.  Articulate how to calculate and increase personal wealth
3.  Create a personal budget
4.  Explain the time value of money
5.  Summarize basic federal income tax information and calculations
6.  Describe the appropriate usages of debt and how to improve credit
7.  Explain how to protect financial information from identity theft
8.  Demonstrate how to select, apply for, manage, and repay student loans
9.  Explain how to prepare for post-graduation success
10.  Dissect the car buying and home buying processes
11.  Recognize the difference between different types of investments
12.  Describe and evaluate different retirement planning opportunities

Class Engagement:
Mastery of the subject matter for this course occurs through taking an active role in the
learning process and therefore students are expected to be actively engaged in this
class. Students perform best in this course if they complete the fillable class notes
that will be made available for each module.
Module Quizzes:
Module Quizzes become available every Monday and must be fully submitted by Sunday
at 11:59pm. Course concepts are communicated through interactive lectures that are
made available every week online. Do not wait until the deadline to start the Module
Quizzes. Unless a University excused absence is received in a timely manner, a 20 point
penalty will be applied for each day late.
Each Module Quiz will have a series of Knowledge Check questions embedded
throughout it and your first attempt at each Knowledge Check question will be
graded. These are intended to confirm your comprehension and retention of the
information in lesson. After submitting your first complete attempt, you will receive a
score which will automatically appear under Grades. You may review each Module
Quiz multiple times to help aid you in exam preparation.
Assignments:
Assignments will become available every Monday (like the Module Quizzes) and will be
due by Sunday at 11:59pm. The purpose of these Assignments is not just to learn
general personal finance theory, but to enable students to apply this knowledge to their
own finances during the semester. You will be notified via Canvas once your Assignment
has been graded. A 20 point penalty will be applied for each day late.

There will be three regular, open note, 60-minuteCanvas exams made up of True/False

Statement on the Family Educational Rights and Privacy
Act (FERPA)
FERPA is a federal law designed to protect the privacy of educational records by limiting
access to these records, to establish the right of students to inspect and review their
educational records, and to provide guidelines for the correction of inaccurate and
misleading data through informal and formal hearings.
Currently enrolled students wishing to withhold any or all directory information items
can do so within howdy.tamu.edu using the Directory Information Withholding Form.
The complete FERPA Notice to Students and the student records policy is available on
the Office of the Registrar webpage.
Items that can never be identified as public information are a student’s social security
number, citizenship, gender, grades, GPR, or class schedule. All efforts will be made in
this class to protect your privacy and to ensure confidential treatment of information
associated with or generated by your participation in the class.
Directory items include name, UIN, local address, permanent address, email address,
local telephone number, permanent telephone number, dates of attendance, program

honors and awards received, participation in officially recognized activities and sports,
medical residence location, and medical residence specialization.
